summary: The last Catskill fire tower to close, in 1990; restored by volunteers and reopened in 2000, it's now staffed weekends by the Red Hill Fire Tower Committee.

facts.design: Aermotor steel tower, 60 ft, with a 7x7 ft steel cab and an unusual 1/2 in. tube alidade

access.note: Volunteer-staffed weekends from Memorial Day to Columbus Day; about a 1-mile hike in.

visit.trail_note: About 1 mile hike to the summit

events.note: Aermotor steel tower built by the state to close a gap in the Catskills' fire-detection network
Closed for good; the last fire tower in the Catskills to go out of service (brief earlier closures in 1971 and the early 1980s, with a return to staffing in 1987)
Registered with the National Historic Lookout Register March 6, 1995, nominated by Bob Spear of FFLA

Reopened to the public after a restoration (begun 1998) by the Catskill Center for Conservation and Development and NYS DEC, funded by state grants matched by local fundraising; NY-NJ Trail Conference volunteers built a new access trail as part of the same effort
Listed on the NRHP September 23, 2001, under the Fire Observation Stations of New York State Forest Preserve multiple-property listing

corrections.proposed: Aermotor steel tower, 60 ft, with a 7x7 ft steel cab
corrections.evidence: NHLR detail page gives the tower's design, height and cab dimensions, which the tower record currently leaves blank.
NHLR describes the tower as 60 ft tall; 60 ft converts to about 18.3 m.
NHLR's most recent visit report (2017) and Wikipedia both describe weekend volunteer staffing by the Red Hill Fire Tower Committee.

notes_for_editor: Sources agree closely; one minor discrepancy: NHLR gives the elevation as 2,980 ft (908 m) while Wikipedia gives 2,990 ft (910 m) — the story uses the NHLR figure and cites it there, not andyarthur.org as originally drafted. The tower record's design, height, staffing and access fields are currently blank/unknown even though NHLR and Wikipedia both support specific values (see corrections). Tried catskillcenter.org's Red Hill fire-tower page directly but it 404'd; Wikipedia and a general web search covered the same restoration history, so it wasn't pursued further within the search budget.
